opus-5.5.text:
I think part of it is historical. Some of the early people at Anthropic, like Jared Kaplan and Sam McCandlish, came from theoretical physics, and people tend to hire people they understand and trust. When you've spent years in a field, you know how to judge whether someone from it is actually good. So there's a network effect.

But I don't think that's the whole story. I think something in physics training actually transfers well to this kind of work.

In physics, especially theoretical physics, you learn to face a very complicated system and ask: what are the few variables that really matter? You don't try to model every detail. You look for scaling behavior, for the right approximation, for the simple law hidden underneath the mess. The scaling-laws work is a very physics-style way of thinking: treat a neural network almost like a physical system, vary the parameters, look at the curves, and find the regularities.

Large models are a bit like that. They're not something we designed line by line and fully understand. They're more like a natural phenomenon we've created and now have to study empirically. So the mindset of an experimental or theoretical physicist, forming hypotheses, designing clean experiments, being comfortable with approximation and with not having a rigorous proof, fits pretty naturally.

There's also a cultural side. Physicists are used to working on very hard problems for a long time without quick feedback, and they're usually not afraid to learn a new field from scratch. When I moved from physics into AI, much of the specific knowledge didn't carry over directly, but the way of thinking did, and the willingness to just sit down and learn the new thing.

So I'd say it's partly who the founders were, and partly that physics trains a kind of taste: knowing what questions to ask about a complex system. That taste turns out to be very useful right now.

r001.rationale: The response mentions early Anthropic members’ physics backgrounds and a resulting network effect, but presents that as only part of the explanation, not the main reason.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that Anthropic hired almost no people without an AI background after Shunyu Yao joined.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there are a few layers to it. The most superficial one is that physicists happen to have the right toolkit. The day-to-day of training large models is a lot of dealing with high-dimensional systems you can't fully understand, where you have to reason from a handful of measurements, find scaling behavior, build simple effective models for messy phenomena. That's basically what a condensed matter or statistical physics education trains you to do. Scaling laws look like critical phenomena. Loss landscapes look like energy landscapes. The vocabulary transfers almost directly.

But I don't think that's really the reason. Lots of fields have good math. I think the deeper thing is a kind of taste, or an attitude toward problems. Physics teaches you to be comfortable not knowing what the right question is yet. You start from a phenomenon, you poke at it, you try to find the simplest explanation that doesn't fall apart, and you're suspicious of anything that only works because of a lot of tuning. Deep learning right now is in exactly that pre-paradigmatic state. There's no textbook that tells you why these things work. So people who are used to doing science without a map tend to do well.

There's also a selection effect that people underrate. Physics as a field has, frankly, more talent than it has interesting, tractable problems at the moment. A lot of very capable people spent ten years learning to think carefully and then found that the frontier of their subfield was moving slowly. AI is the opposite: the frontier moves every month and the gap between what we can build and what we understand is enormous. For someone trained to care about understanding, that gap is irresistible. I count myself in that group. I didn't leave physics because I stopped liking it. I left because this felt like the place where a physicist's way of thinking was most needed and least present.

And specifically for Anthropic, I think the culture matters. The company has a very strong orientation toward "we should actually understand what's going on inside these models," which is the interpretability side, and toward being honest about uncertainty. That resonates with physicists. We're trained to say "I don't know" and to distinguish between a result and a story about a result. In a field full of hype, that habit is valuable, and I think the people doing hiring recognize it, partly because many of them came from physics themselves. So it becomes self-reinforcing: physicists hire people who think like them, and the environment keeps rewarding that style.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the hiring pattern to physicists’ skills, problem-solving style, talent availability, and Anthropic’s culture. It does not identify the technical founders’ physics connections as the main reason.

astra-6.text:
I don’t know their actual hiring rationale, but my guess is that physics trains people to work in a way that’s useful for understanding large models. You have a complicated system, you can’t derive everything from first principles, so you run experiments, look for regularities, and try to build a simpler explanation of what’s happening.

That’s quite relevant to AI today. We know how to train these models, but we don’t fully understand why certain capabilities emerge or why particular interventions work. You need people who can move between mathematical intuition and empirical evidence—and who are willing to change their theory when the experiment disagrees.

So I’d interpret it less as physics knowledge being directly applicable and more as a certain research habit being valuable. Whether that’s what motivated Anthropic specifically, though, I can only speculate.

sol-6.1.text:
My guess is that physics trains people to work on problems where you don’t have a clear recipe. You build a model, make a prediction, run an experiment, and then figure out why reality disagrees with you. A lot of research on language models has that character. We can train these systems, but we still don’t fully understand why certain things work or how particular behaviors emerge.

There’s also a practical reason: physicists often have strong mathematical and computational skills, so they can move into machine learning fairly naturally. And once you have a few people from that background, their networks probably influence who joins next. But I don’t know Anthropic’s internal hiring decisions—that’s just my interpretation.
